prompt: You gave a reading app your shop password, and now you want to stop it using your account. What does that cost you?
hint: A password is the same key for everybody who holds it.

choices.text: Nothing much: you revoke the app's own token on the shop's account settings page
choices.why: That is what delegation gives you. With a password there is no token of the app's own to revoke.

choices.text: Uninstalling the app, which deletes the password
choices.why: The app may have stored it on its own server, which uninstalling does not reach.

choices.text: A new password, which also cuts off every other app that had the old one
choices.why: Right. The password is the only lever, and pulling it stops everything that held it at once.

choices.text: Waiting a few minutes for the app's access to expire on its own, as tokens do
choices.why: Access tokens expire; a password does not, so the app keeps working until it is changed.

prompt: Match each OAuth role to what plays it in this lesson's lab.
hint: One file plays two of them.

prompt: Why does OAuth trust the browser least of all the parties in a flow?
hint: Think about who else can see what passes through it.

choices.text: It runs the client's code, so it holds the client's secret
choices.why: A web app's secret stays on the app's server; the browser never receives it.

choices.text: Extensions, history and logs see what passes through it
choices.why: Right. That is why nothing the browser carries is enough on its own.

choices.text: It cannot keep a cookie between the redirect and the callback
choices.why: It can; the client's session cookie survives the whole flow. The problem is who else reads the addresses.

choices.text: It is the resource owner, and owners are never trusted
choices.why: The person is the resource owner; the browser only carries messages for them.

prompt: Put the authorization code flow in order.
hint: The browser half comes first.
items: The client redirects the browser to `/authorize`
The person signs in and agrees at the authorization server
The browser returns to the callback with a code and `state`
The client exchanges the code at `/token`
The client calls the API with the access token
trap: Exchanging the code before checking `state` lets a code from somebody else's session in.

prompt: Why does the authorization server send a code through the browser, and not the access token itself?
hint: Where do redirect addresses end up?

choices.text: A code is short enough to fit in an address, and a full token is not
choices.why: Tokens fit in addresses; the implicit grant put them there. The question is who reads the address.

choices.text: A token would expire before the browser finished following the redirect
choices.why: A token lasts minutes, and a redirect takes milliseconds.

choices.text: The browser has somewhere to store a code but nowhere to keep a token
choices.why: A browser can keep either; storage is not the issue.

choices.text: Addresses leak, and a leaked code is useless without the second request
choices.why: Right. The code works once, for a minute, and only with the client's credentials and the verifier.

prompt: A client is registered as `https://app.example`, and its authorization server accepts any `redirect_uri` that starts with that string. Which address could then receive a code?
hint: Read the comparison as a string, not as a URL.

choices.text: `https://app.example.other.test/cb`, on another host
choices.why: Right. The prefix matches and the host is different. That is why the comparison has to be exact.

choices.text: Only `https://app.example/cb`, since a URL's host must match
choices.why: A prefix check compares characters and knows nothing about hosts.

choices.text: None, because a code is only issued after the client sends its secret
choices.why: The secret is checked at `/token`, after the code has already been sent.

choices.text: `http://app.example/cb`, because the scheme is ignored
choices.why: `http://` does not start with `https://`, so this one fails the prefix.

prompt: `pkce.py` printed a verifier of 64 characters. How many characters long is its S256 challenge?
hint: A SHA-256 is 32 bytes, whatever went in.

prompt: `idp.py` gives no code unless the request carries `code_challenge_method=___`.
hint: The other method sends the verifier itself.

prompt: A web app on a server already sends its client secret to `/token`. What does PKCE add for it?
hint: Think of a code that arrives in the wrong session.

choices.text: Nothing at all; PKCE was written for public clients and only applies to them
choices.why: RFC 9700 asks every client to use it, and the OAuth 2.1 draft requires it.

choices.text: It replaces the client secret, so the app stops storing a secret anywhere
choices.why: The two protect different things, and a confidential client keeps both.

choices.text: A code slipped into another person's session fails on that session's verifier
choices.why: Right. The secret proves which client is asking; the verifier proves which sign-in the code came from.

choices.text: It encrypts the code in the redirect, so the browser cannot read it on the way
choices.why: The code travels in clear in the address; PKCE adds a proof at `/token`, not encryption.

prompt: Which of these does `idp.py` do that no real authorization server does?
hint: It is the one shortcut that lets `curl` drive it.

choices.text: Signs every token it issues with RS256 and a 2048-bit RSA key
choices.why: RS256 is what most real servers use.

choices.text: Refuses a `redirect_uri` it does not know, without redirecting the browser
choices.why: Every correct authorization server does this.

choices.text: Publishes its public key at a JWKS address for APIs and clients
choices.why: That is OpenID Connect's standard way of handing out keys.

choices.text: Answers `/authorize` at once, as a user who is always signed in and agrees
choices.why: Right. A real one shows a sign-in page and a consent screen the person can refuse.

prompt: Why is `idp-key.pem` written with permissions `0600`?
hint: What could somebody do with a copy of it?

choices.text: Python refuses to load a key that others can read
choices.why: Python loads it whatever the permissions; the restriction is for people.

choices.text: Whoever reads it signs tokens that every trusting API accepts
choices.why: Right. The private key is the server's whole authority.

choices.text: The JWKS endpoint serves this file, so it must not change
choices.why: The JWKS carries the public half only, built from the key in memory.

choices.text: So that every restart creates a fresh key
choices.why: Permissions decide who reads it; the program reuses the same key at every start.

prompt: You ask `/books/stock` with no `Authorization` header. What does `idp.py` answer?
hint: The API cannot tell who you are yet.

choices.text: 403, because no token means no scope
choices.why: 403 is for a valid token that lacks a scope; here there is no token at all.

choices.text: 401, with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
choices.why: Right. The header tells the client which kind of credential to bring.

choices.text: 302 to `/authorize`
choices.why: An API answers with a status; sending a browser to sign in is the client's job.

choices.text: 400, because the request is malformed
choices.why: The request is well formed; it only lacks a credential.

prompt: You exchange a code a second time, with the right verifier and the right secret. What happens?
hint: When does `idp.py` take a code out of its table?

choices.text: 200 and a fresh set of tokens
choices.why: That would make a copied code as good as the original, every time.

choices.text: 200 and the same tokens as the first exchange
choices.why: The server keeps no record of tokens it issued for a code.

choices.text: 401 `invalid_client`, because the secret was already used
choices.why: A client secret can be used any number of times; it is the code that works once.

choices.text: 400 `invalid_grant`
choices.why: Right. The first exchange took the code out of the table, so it is unknown now.

prompt: Most errors at `/authorize` go back to the client's callback with `error=`. Why does an unregistered `redirect_uri` get a 400 from `idp.py` itself instead?
hint: Which address would the redirect go to?

choices.text: The address is the thing in doubt, so a redirect would message whoever is there
choices.why: Right. The other errors can go back because the address is known to be the client's.

choices.text: A 302 carries a code in its address, but it has no room for an error
choices.why: The `invalid_scope` refusal was a 302 carrying `error=invalid_scope`.

choices.text: The callback would call `/authorize` again, and the browser would loop
choices.why: A callback does not call `/authorize`; nothing loops.

choices.text: OAuth forbids redirecting for every kind of error at `/authorize`, not just this one
choices.why: It forbids them for this one; the others redirect, as the lab showed.

prompt: A token granted `openid email` asks for `/books/stock`. What comes back?
hint: The token is genuine and in date.

choices.text: 401 `invalid_token`
choices.why: The signature, issuer, audience and time all pass; nothing is wrong with the token itself.

choices.text: 200, since any valid token reads the stock
choices.why: The endpoint needs `books:read`, and this token was never granted it.

choices.text: 403 `insufficient_scope`, naming `books:read`
choices.why: Right. A valid token without the scope is 403, and `WWW-Authenticate` names what was missing.

choices.text: 400 `invalid_scope`
choices.why: That is `/authorize` refusing a request; an API answers 401 or 403.

prompt: What does the scope on an access token decide?
hint: Lesson 11 is about the other half.

choices.text: Which client the token was issued to, and on whose behalf
choices.why: That is `client_id`, a separate claim.

choices.text: Exactly what the person is allowed to do inside the API
choices.why: The API still applies its own rules; a banned account opens nothing whatever the scope.

choices.text: How long the token stays valid
choices.why: That is `exp`, and `expires_in` in the response.

choices.text: An upper limit, which the API's own rules narrow further
choices.why: Right. A scope is what the client asked for and the person agreed to, an upper limit and no more.

prompt: The authorization server may grant less than was asked, so a client reads the ___ field of the token response.
hint: It was `books:read openid profile` in the first flow.

prompt: Match each check on an ID token to what it stops.
hint: Each one closes a different door.

pairs.left: the signature, with the key the `kid` names

pairs.right: a token made out to somebody else

pairs.left: `nonce` is the one this client sent
pairs.right: an ID token replayed from an earlier sign-in
a token kept and used later

right_distractors: a person who typed the wrong password

prompt: An app signs people in by calling an API with whatever access token it receives and reading the user id the API returns. What is wrong with that?
hint: Who else could hold an access token for the same person?

choices.text: Access tokens expire far too quickly to keep anybody signed in for a whole session
choices.why: The app would keep its own session after sign-in; lifetime is not the flaw.

choices.text: Another app's token for that person works too, letting that app sign in as them
choices.why: Right. An access token's audience is the API, and nothing in it says which app should accept it. An ID token's audience is the app.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong, as long as the API checks every token's signature
choices.why: The signature proves the token is genuine, not that it was issued to this app.

choices.text: The user id differs for every client, so it identifies nobody in particular
choices.why: The API returns the same subject whichever token brings it; that is what makes the flaw usable.

prompt: OpenID Connect's discovery document is at `/.well-known/___` under the issuer.
hint: `check_token.py` reads it first.

prompt: `check_token.py` refused the access token, given the audience `shelf-web`, with `Audience doesn't match`. What was in the token's `aud`?
hint: Who is an access token made out to?

choices.text: `shelf-web`, with a different issuer
choices.why: An issuer mismatch has its own error; this one is about the audience.

choices.text: Nothing, because access tokens carry no audience
choices.why: `idp.py`'s access tokens carry one, and the check read it.

choices.text: `shelf-api`
choices.why: Right. Checked with `shelf-api`, the same token passed and showed its scope.

choices.text: The nonce the client sent at `/authorize`
choices.why: A nonce goes into the ID token, never into `aud`.

prompt: With rotation, a refresh token that was already exchanged comes back to `/token`. What does `idp.py` do?
hint: It cannot tell which holder is the real app.

choices.text: Refuses it and leaves its replacement working
choices.why: Then the thief might be the one holding the replacement. The server ends both.

choices.text: Accepts it once more, since it was valid a moment ago
choices.why: A rotated refresh token works once; that is the whole mechanism.

choices.text: Refuses it and ends the whole grant, replacement included
choices.why: Right. Both holders lose, and the person signs in again.

choices.text: Revokes every access token already issued in that grant
choices.why: It cannot: the first access token still opened the stock list, because the API asks nobody.

prompt: `idp.py`'s access tokens last 300 seconds. A client keeps working for one hour, refreshing each time a token runs out. How many access tokens does it use in that hour, the first included?
hint: An hour is 3600 seconds.

prompt: A single-page app needs to keep a person signed in for days. Which arrangement does the lesson prefer?
hint: The best place for the token is the one the page's scripts cannot reach.

choices.text: The client secret in the app's JavaScript, to authenticate each refresh
choices.why: A secret shipped in JavaScript is in every copy; a public client has none worth the name.

choices.text: A refresh token in `localStorage`, rotated on every use
choices.why: The lesson allows this only if the browser must hold it. The preferred answer keeps it out of the browser.

choices.text: The refresh token in the address after `#`, so it never reaches a server
choices.why: That is where the implicit grant put tokens, and history and logs can read it.

choices.text: The app's own small server keeps them, and the browser gets a cookie
choices.why: Right. A backend for frontend keeps the refresh token where no script in the page can read it.

prompt: Which of these were in `idp.py`'s answer to a `client_credentials` request? Choose all that apply.
hint: A machine can always ask again, and nobody signed in.

choices.text: `access_token`
choices.why: Right. That is the point of the request.

choices.text: `refresh_token`
choices.why: The client can repeat the request; a refresh token would be a second credential protecting nothing.

choices.text: `expires_in`
choices.why: Right. 300, like every access token from this server.

choices.text: `id_token`
choices.why: Nobody signed in, so there is nobody for an ID token to describe.

prompt: A nightly job with no person involved asks `/token` for a token with `grant_type=___`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: A support tool uses client credentials to change customers' addresses for them. What does that get wrong?
hint: Look at `sub` in a machine token.

choices.text: Every change is logged as the tool's own, and no log says for whom
choices.why: Right. The token's `sub` is the client, and every record after that is wrong about who.

choices.text: The authorization server refuses, since client credentials carry no scope
choices.why: Client credentials tokens carry a scope; `idp.py` granted `books:read`.

choices.text: Each customer must consent on a screen before every single change
choices.why: There is no consent in this grant at all; that is part of the problem.

choices.text: The token expires before the change reaches the database and is saved
choices.why: Five minutes is plenty for one request.

prompt: Why does RFC 9700 say the implicit grant should not be used?
hint: Where did it put the token?

choices.text: It needs the user's password, typed into the app's own form
choices.why: That is the password grant. The implicit grant used the same redirect as the code flow.

choices.text: It put the access token in the redirect, where logs and history read it
choices.why: Right. The front channel carried the token itself, and there was no refresh token either.

choices.text: It carried no scopes, so every token it returned opened the whole account
choices.why: It carried scopes like any other grant.

choices.text: It requires a client secret, which a browser has no way to keep
choices.why: It required no secret; that is part of why it was made for browsers.

prompt: An old tutorial's app posts the user's password to `/token` with `grant_type=password`. What does `idp.py` answer?
hint: It is not a grant this server knows.

choices.text: 200 with an access token and no refresh token
choices.why: That is what the grant once returned; this server does not offer it.

choices.text: 401 `invalid_client`
choices.why: The client authenticated correctly; the grant type is what was refused.

choices.text: 400 `unsupported_grant_type`
choices.why: Right, with `password is not offered here`.

choices.text: 302 to the callback with an error
choices.why: `/token` is a direct request and never redirects.

prompt: Put a SAML sign-in with the browser POST binding in order.
hint: The two servers never talk directly.
items: The browser asks the service provider for a page
The service provider redirects the browser with a `SAMLRequest`
The person signs in at the identity provider
The identity provider returns a form holding the signed assertion
The browser posts the assertion to the service provider
The service provider checks it and starts a session
trap: The assertion reaches the service provider through the browser, never from the identity provider directly.

prompt: `xmlsec1` printed `OK` for an assertion. Which of these must the service provider still check itself? Choose all that apply.
hint: `xmlsec1` checks signatures and knows nothing of SAML.

choices.text: That the digest of the signed element matches
choices.why: That is part of what `OK` reported.

choices.text: That `Audience` names this service provider
choices.why: Right. An assertion for another application is validly signed too.

choices.text: That the time now is inside `NotBefore` and `NotOnOrAfter`
choices.why: Right. The lab's assertion was outside its window and still printed `OK`.

choices.text: That the assertion's `ID` has not been seen before
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the same assertion can be posted twice.

choices.text: That the signature value decodes as base64
choices.why: Verifying it required decoding it; `OK` covers that.

prompt: Match each SAML term to its nearest counterpart in OpenID Connect.
hint: The roles map across even though the formats do not.

prompt: A company's staff sign in to a tool it bought, through the company's identity provider, and the browser posts a signed XML document to the tool. Which protocol is that?
hint: Only one of them speaks XML.

choices.text: OpenID Connect
choices.why: It signs people in too, but with a JWT, not XML.

choices.text: OAuth 2.0 client credentials
choices.why: No person signs in with client credentials.

choices.text: SAML 2.0
choices.why: Right. An assertion posted through the browser is SAML's POST binding.

choices.text: PKCE
choices.why: PKCE is a protection inside the OAuth code flow, not a protocol of its own.

prompt: In your first job, a team asks you to add "Sign in with Google" to a web app. What is your part, according to this lesson?
hint: Somebody else runs the authorization server.

choices.text: Writing an authorization server like `idp.py`, but hardened for production use
choices.why: Google is the authorization server; writing one is exactly what the lesson says not to do.

choices.text: Setting up a library and the provider correctly, and the checks it runs
choices.why: Right. Configuration and those checks are where integrations go wrong.

choices.text: Storing the users' Google passwords, hashed as lesson 10 describes
choices.why: The app never sees a Google password; that is the point of delegation.

choices.text: Accepting Google's access token as proof of who signed in
choices.why: That is the confusion the OpenID Connect section refused; the ID token is the proof.

prompt: Put what a client does with an ID token, before trusting it, in order.
hint: It cannot check a signature before it has the key.
items: Read the discovery document to find `jwks_uri`
Fetch the key the token's `kid` names
Verify the signature, accepting RS256 only
Compare `nonce` with the one it sent
trap: Reading claims before the signature is checked means reading what anybody could have written.

prompt: A grant is revoked at 10:07:00 because a refresh token came back twice. The thief's newest access token was issued at 10:05:00 and lasts 300 seconds. For how many seconds after the revocation does it still open an API that checks only the signature and the time?
hint: Revoking the grant does not reach a token the API checks on its own.

prompt: A phone app uses the code flow with PKCE and has no client secret. Another app on the phone receives the redirect and the code. What stops it?
hint: Which value never passed through the redirect?

choices.text: The authorization server's check of `state` on the way back
choices.why: `state` is checked by the client that sent it, not by the authorization server.

choices.text: It lacks the verifier, which never left the real app
choices.why: Right. The challenge it may have seen cannot be run backwards into the verifier.

choices.text: The `redirect_uri` comparison that `/token` makes
choices.why: The other app received the redirect at the registered address, so that comparison passes.

choices.text: Nothing; a client without a secret cannot be protected at all
choices.why: That was the situation before RFC 7636; PKCE exists for exactly this client.

prompt: You review an OAuth integration. Which of these findings are defects? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them are what this lesson recommends.

choices.text: A `redirect_uri` registered with a wildcard
choices.why: Right. Only an exact match keeps codes away from addresses the client does not control.

choices.text: Access tokens that expire after five minutes
choices.why: That is the recommended shape: short access tokens, refreshed.

choices.text: The password grant switched on
choices.why: Right. RFC 9700 says it must not be used.

choices.text: Refresh tokens rotated on every use
choices.why: Rotation is what lets the server notice a stolen copy.

choices.text: The app signs users in by reading the access token
choices.why: Right. Signing in is the ID token's job, checked for `aud` and `nonce`.
